name: Massicot Yellow
lede: Massicot is a yellow oxide of lead, one of the oldest painters' yellows, and a pale, creamy one on screen.

sections.title: The material
sections.body:
Massicot is lead(II) oxide, PbO, and as a mineral it forms soft yellow scaly or earthy masses near lead ore deposits [1]. The mineral was first described by Huot in 1841, and it is the form that is stable above about 540°C, the high-temperature twin of litharge [1]. The word probably comes from an Arabic term for Egyptian alum or soda [1].

Painters made it long before mineralogists named it. Pastoureau notes that heating ceruse, or lead white, gave massicot (yellow) or minium (red), depending on the temperature [2]. Lead pigments could not sit beside sulfur-based ones such as orpiment or vermilion, or the whites turned grey and then blackish [2].

sections.title: A blanket name
sections.body: Massicot was not a precise term. Ball cites Merrifield that it also went by the name giallorino, and thinks it wisest to read that as a blanket word for any lead-bearing yellow [3]. Medieval painters also used lead-tin yellows, and were probably often confused with lead antimonate in the records [3]. Maerz and Paul record massicot as a color name from 1472 [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our swatch is the Ridgway and ISCC-NBS color, a pale cream-yellow, not the raw pigment [4]. 190 of 23,781 paintings, 0.8%, have a patch of it covering at least 5% of the canvas, as photographed [5]. The top match is Toriyama Sekien's *Courtesan and Cherry Branch* (1781), about 67% [5]. Related names: [[orpiment]], [[lemon-yellow]] and [[beige]].
